Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran , which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz. Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel. In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month. Although the law, named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, called for new penalties on Russia starting next week, it also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so. Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action undercuts the Graham Act's main goal and will fuel Russia's "desire to keep killing people." The US diesel deal with Russia and the waiver are the latest steps in what Zelenskiy said he expects to be continued sanctions relief on Moscow. The prospect of the US continuing to pressure Russia to end the war has dimmed since Graham's death in July, Zelenskiy said. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and a confidant of Trump, strongly supported Ukraine. "It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," the Ukrainian president wrote. HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly [USN:L4N45Z20E TEXT:"Russian attack"] on the capital. Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters. Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off. Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was [USN:L8N46213X TEXT:"disrupted"] after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"an order originating from the White House"], Reuters reported on Thursday. The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration. Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"argue that"] Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow. Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy. “Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.”

item.title: What redistricting means for Tennessee voters
item.description: Redrawing congressional district lines splits neighbors and groups them with people far away.
item.dc:creator: Ally J. Levine, Bianca Flowers, David Hood-Nuño
item.content:encoded: It’s a political fault line that leaves neighbors on both sides with less say. 9th District5th District The street outside Tammy Jo O'Neal's home has become a political boundary with big implications. The city of Memphis used to sit almost entirely in one congressional district. The new map splits O'Neal from neighbors across the street, each now belonging to districts with voters halfway across the state who have different needs and interests. O'Neal sees the new map as more than a split block. “There's this divide that's happening in our lives,not just in our districts.” District 5 District 9 Tammy Jo O’Neal sits for a portrait on the front porch of their home on Elzey Ave in Memphis, Tennessee, US, July 29, 2026. REUTERS/Seth Herald A citydivided By Bianca Flowers , David Hood-Nuño and Ally J. Levine Published Oct. 17, 2026 6:00 a.m. EDT What happens when congressional district lines are redrawn, splitting neighbors and grouping them with people far away Four years before the Memphis redistricting, Republicans used a similar strategy in drawing new maps for Nashville. They split the city, which had voted overwhelmingly Democratic for roughly 70 years, into three broader districts where Republicans can now easily prevail. Battles over redistricting have long been intertwined with racism and political power, particularly in southern states like Tennessee. Sixty-four years ago, a federal court found Tennessee diluted voting power in urban areas where majority Black voters lived and ordered the legislature to redraw its congressional districts. For decades, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was a powerful tool for Black voters, particularly in the South, to challenge discrimination and protect political power among people of color to elect representatives who would advocate for their communities. The act significantly increased Black and Hispanic representation in Congress by curtailing certain redistricting practices, including splitting people of color among many districts or concentrating them in some districts to limit their impact in others. But those protections have been steadily weakened. In 2013, when Democrat Barack Obama was president, the Supreme Court’s decision on the Alabama case Shelby County v. Holder gutted a provision requiring federal approval before states change voting laws or political maps. In April, the court narrowed the Voting Rights Act further in Louisiana v. Callais , making it harder to challenge new maps that dilute the voting power of communities of color. The court essentially required such challenges to prove that districts were drawn intentionally to discriminate on the basis of race, and not for other reasons. Republicans argue their redistricting in Tennessee and elsewhere is about party politics, not race. They point out that Democrats regularly redraw districts in states they control to give their party easier election wins. Democrats have done the same in California, for example, said Steve Hickey, chair of the Republican Party in Williamson County, a popular suburban area south of Nashville. “This is part of a bigger game being played nationally, and I don’t think it’s fair to say that this was done to gut” the Voting Rights Act, he said. Redistricting in the United States is generally controlled by state legislatures, which adjust voter maps after the once-a-decade census. Both parties have historically used the process to help their candidates win future elections. In 2025, at the urging of President Donald Trump, Texas launched an unusual mid-decade redistricting drive as part of a broader Republican push to gain congressional seats in half a dozen states, including Tennessee. Democrats responded with their own partisan redistricting in California and attempts that faltered in other states. Civil rights activists say Tennessee’s congressional districts, all of which currently favor Republicans, are now a testing ground for dismantling voting rights protections across the United States. “This lack of competition spills over and has racial implications,” said John Geer, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University who conducts polling in Tennessee. Reuters sought to quantify the impact of redistricting on the voters of Tennessee, examining public funding, demographics and socioeconomic factors to show why it’s important to residents when a city is split up like this. MemphisDistrict 9Suburbs of NashvilleDistrict 5District 8District 9 Population by race, one dot per person Black residents White residents Other races and ethnicities Memphis has the largest Black population in Tennessee. The city of some 630,000 people is 63% Black. Memphis accounted for 78% of the former District 9’s population, making it the only majority-Black district in the state. Earlier this year, the Tennessee legislature drew new district lines, splitting Memphis and its Black communities into three separate districts. The pieces of the city are now grouped with rural and suburban Tennesseans in districts that reach halfway across the state. Note: “White” and “Black” are non-Hispanic. “Other races and ethnicities” combines Hispanic or Latino residents of any race with the non-Hispanic categories Asian alone, American Indian and Alaska Native alone, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone, Some Other Race alone, and Two or More Races. Sources: US Census Bureau (2020 census redistricting data; TIGER/Line boundaries); Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 districts); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 districts); State of Tennessee and the City of Memphis Engineering Division (city limits); Tennessee Department of Transportation (roads) Reuters spoke to more than 35 redistricting scholars, political analysts, civic leaders, political candidates and voters about the consequences of redistricting for the most vulnerable communities in Tennessee’s two biggest cities. Cities faced the biggest impact because rural areas were already represented by a Republican and continue to be so after the redistricting, albeit in districts with different demographics. Before redistricting, both Nashville and Memphis were overwhelmingly Democratic districts in an otherwise Republican state. In 2024, District 9, including most of Memphis, went 71% for Democrat Steve Cohen. In 2020, Jim Cooper, a Democrat, ran unopposed in Nashville’s District 5, winning more than 99% of votes cast. In 2022, the new District 5 flipped, with the Republican candidate winning 57%. Tennessee’s new maps have combined city, suburban and rural populations that have widely varying needs and political preferences. The residents of Nashville and Memphis, for instance, are far more likely to struggle with poverty, housing, public safety and related issues. Residents there could now struggle to elect Congress members who prioritize policies to address these issues, according to Odessa Kelly, executive director of Stand Up Nashville, a nonprofit community organization that advocates for racial and economic equality. She said Black voters in Nashville no longer felt they had someone to stand up for them in Congress, from federal funding going to the city to critical votes on bills that directly affect city residents. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention developed the Social Vulnerability Index to gauge how well a community can withstand and recover from an emergency, and to identify which communities may need the most support. Shelby County, home to Memphis, ranks among the most vulnerable of Tennessee’s 95 counties on various indicators such as housing cost burden and lack of access to a vehicle. Memphis, Nashville residents rank higher in social vulnerability A US government index compares Tennessee communities on socioeconomic and demographic factors gauging their resilience to unexpected hardships. 25th 50th 75th 100th percentile Lower vulnerability Higher vulnerability Shelby County (Memphis) Minority status Racial or ethnic minority 100 Davidson County (Nashville) Housing and transportation In structures of 10+ units 97 No vehicle available 94 More people than rooms 60 Lives in group quarters 56 Mobile homes 0 Household characteristics Aged 17 and under 97 Single-parent household 96 Speaks English less than well 91 With a disability 9 Aged 65 and over 5 Socioeconomic status Housing cost burdened 100 Unemployed 86 No health insurance 76 Below 150% of poverty 50 No high school diploma (25+) 16 0 Chart showing where Shelby County and Davidson County rank among Tennessee’s 95 counties on 16 measures of the CDC’s Social Vulnerability Index, grouped into four themes, on a scale from the 0 to the 100th percentile with the other 93 counties as faint ticks. Both rank high on most measures — Shelby at the 100th percentile for racial or ethnic minority share and housing cost burden, Davidson at the 100th for apartments in large buildings and for people who speak English less than well. Both drop to the middle or bottom on poverty, the 50th percentile for Shelby and the 23rd for Davidson, and on residents aged 65 and over. Source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry Social Vulnerability Index 2022 In 2024, just over a third of Tennessee voters picked Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, and in 2020, Democrats won two congressional seats out of the state’s nine, carrying Nashville and Memphis. Now, every congressional district in Tennessee is considered “safe” for Republicans. Sandi Wells, a self-described “very conservative” voter from Williamson County, just outside Nashville, said it was “kind of odd” to group Memphis in the same district with parts of Williamson County 200 miles away. But she rejected the notion that districts should be drawn to protect Black voting power. “I don’t think we should have districts that are based on race,” she said. “I mean, that’s just ridiculous for anyone to even think that we should have that.” Shane Tinnin, a 52-year-old small business owner who maintains homes in both cities and has voted mostly for Democrats, understands that parties seek political power through redistricting but called the Memphis maps a particularly striking setback for Black political power. “In Nashville, it seemed really more like this is a political move,” he said, noting that it was not a Black-majority city. “When you do it in Memphis, where it’s an even more liberal district, but also a predominantly Black district, it just feels especially egregious to me.” Odessa Kelly, executive director at Stand Up Nashville, points to topics of focus for her and her team at a meeting in July. REUTERS/Seth Herald Volunteers for The Equity Alliance canvass through neighborhoods in Memphis to do “accountability” door knocks to speak with residents about elected officials following the GOP-led effort to redistrict the city. REUTERS/Seth Herald Securing funding Reuters examined how Nashville’s redistricting has impacted community project funding, under which lawmakers can seek federal money for local projects. Previously known as earmarks, community project funds returned to Congress with a more transparent process in fiscal year 2022 after a decade-long moratorium. A Reuters analysis found a dramatic shift in funding for Nashville after the city was split among three districts. Jim Cooper, a Democrat, steered most of the old 5th District’s project funding to Nashville in fiscal years 2022 and 2023. In the years since, only a small share of funding has gone toward projects in the city, including fiscal year 2027 requests still pending before Congress. Funding can vary greatly between representatives. Only John Rose, who currently represents the 6th District, has requested funding among the three members whose districts included Nashville after redistricting. Matt Van Epps and Andy Ogles have not pursued community project funding for their districts at all, arguing against such spending on principle. All three did not provide a comment or did not respond to a request to comment. Total Community Project Funding for districts that include Nashville After FY2023 FY2024 $18 mln $21 mln $2.5 mln Not Nashville $18 mln Nashville Nashville $3 mln $15.5 mln Before Two flow diagrams comparing Community Project Funds before and after redistricting. In the year before, when Nashville sat in a single district, District 5 received $18 million and $15.5 million of it went to Nashville, with $2.5 million going elsewhere. In the year after, with Nashville divided across three districts, Districts 5, 6 and 7 received $21 million between them but only $3 million reached Nashville, while $18 million went to areas outside the city. Note: Data show the total funding for districts that include Nashville. Before the 2022 redistricting, Nashville was contained in District 5. After, it was split between Districts 5, 6 and 7. Source: US Government Accountability Office The shift away from community funding jeopardized future funding for projects like public housing, healthcare centers, buildings for the two historically Black colleges in the city and public transportation in Nashville. For Memphis, a similar decline in earmark funding would be a big loss. Since 2022, District 9 Representative Steve Cohen, a Democrat, pulled in $52.6 million for projects based in Memphis, according to figures published by the US Government Accountability Office and the US House Committee on Appropriations. That’s 83% of all the community project funding for District 9 in that period. District 7 State capitol District 6 State House of Representatives The Tennessee State Capitol building and Legislative Plaza, which is undergoing construction. REUTERS/Seth Herald Another important role for a member of Congress is to act as a middleman between people in their district and the government, helping negotiate the bureaucracy of Washington. When Cooper represented Nashville, he fielded calls about immigration paperwork, passports, Medicare, Social Security checks and more, said Tennessee State Senator Charlane Oliver, who worked as a community liaison and communications staffer in Cooper’s congressional office from 2017 to 2019. “He would show up to the cookout, the fish fry, the parades, the meetings and the galas,” she said. That kind of interaction is harder if the representative does not have a local office. When Nashville was split, only one representative, Mark Green of District 7, kept an office near the center of the city. That office was closed when Van Epps took over the seat in 2025, leaving no offices within the city limits. Constituents in Nashville have to drive 36 miles on average to visit a congressional district office, a Reuters analysis found, compared with less than 10 miles when Cooper represented Nashville, the seat of Davidson County. Average trip to Congressional district office District 5 +39 miles after District 6 +17 mi District 7 +16 mi 0 10 20 30 40 50 miles 9 miles before redistricting A chart of the average driving distance for Nashville residents to their closest congressional district office, shown for each of the three districts the city is now split among. A dark bar common to all three marks the 9-mile average from when Nashville sat in a single district, flagged on the scale as “9 miles before redistricting.” A lighter bar extends past it to each district’s new average: District 5 adds 39 miles, reaching about 47; District 6 adds 17, reaching about 25; and District 7 adds 16, reaching about 24 miles. Note: Data shows the average driving distance for Nashville residents in each district to their closest district office. District 7’s offices are those open under Rep. Matt Van Epps, who won the seat after Mark Green resigned in 2025. Green kept an office in downtown Nashville; which put District 7’s average at 5 miles. That office no longer exists. Source: Reuters analysis of congressional district office locations Van Epps and the other two Republicans running this year in Nashville districts, Johnny Garrett and Charlie Hatcher, did not respond to Reuters requests for interviews for this story. Most city buses don’t operate far enough outside the city to visit a congressional district office in Cookeville, more than an hour’s drive away. Kyle Cook, who works in the public library, said Cooper’s office used to be just upstairs from his own in downtown Nashville. “Now, if I wanted to advocate just as a regular citizen for better busing, I would have to call this office in Cookeville and it’s just not the same kind of relationship,” Cook said. Who speaks for Memphis? Cohen represented Memphis for 19 years but stood down when new maps were passed, saying “these districts were drawn to beat me.” State Representative Justin Pearson, a progressive Democrat, is campaigning to represent the 9th District. Pearson gained national attention in 2023 when he was temporarily expelled from the Tennessee House, for what Republicans described as a breach of decorum when he joined a protest on gun control . Polls show him trailing Brent Taylor, a Republican state senator endorsed by President Donald Trump. But Pearson said Tennessee was “not a lost cause” for Democrats. In an interview with Reuters, Pearson described the Memphis redistricting as “one of the most significant political deprivations of Black political power and accessibility to the ballot since the end of Reconstruction in Tennessee.” Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson stands for a portrait in the Cooper Young neighborhood in Memphis. REUTERS/Seth Herald Taylor has defended redistricting efforts in Tennessee as a “compliance measure” in response to the 2026 US Supreme Court ruling that he says prohibits the consideration of racial data when redrawing political boundaries. Asked about his top priorities in such a diverse district spanning downtown Memphis to rural Fayette County, Taylor pointed to inflation. “Everybody feels the pain right now,” he said. “When I filled up my car the other day, it was $112. People feel the pinch at the gas pump. They feel higher prices when they go to the grocery store. Everything we do costs more.” Civil Miller-Watkins, an eighth-grade math teacher in Fayette County who was drawn into District 9 and plans to vote for Pearson, said the needs of voters in her area differ from those in Memphis. Rural voters worry about access to broadband, ambulances, grocery stores and schools, she said. “All of these interests are very legitimate,” Miller-Watkins said. “But I don’t know if any community can say they’re going to have effective representation.” Pearson, the Democrat, says he’s campaigned in 15 counties that now come under the district and economic hardship is the common thread. “That’s hurting people who are working class in Memphis, just like it’s hurting farmers in Savannah, Tennessee,” he said. “We have a lot more in common.” Urban 96% Suburban 4% Shelby County 737,000 people live in an urban county in District 9 Tipton County 31,000 live in a suburban county District 9 After Urban 35% Suburban 27% Memphis Nashville Williamson 107k Shelby 269k people Rutherford 39k Maury 33k Memphis area Small towns 22% Bedford 50k Lincoln 35k McNairy 26k Giles 30k Hardeman 25k Marshall 34k Lawrence 44k Hardin 27k Wayne 16k Moore 7k Rural 16% Before redistricting Fayette 25k Two panels comparing the counties that make up Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District before and after the 2026 redraw, with each county drawn at an area proportional to its population. Before, the district is almost entirely one place: urban Shelby County, home to Memphis, fills the panel with roughly 737,000 people, beside a thin sliver for suburban Tipton County’s ~31,000. After, 767,872 people are spread across 15 counties in four groups. Urban counties make up 35% of the district; suburban counties comprise 27%, small towns 22% and rural counties 16%. Note: Counties are grouped by the National Center for Health Statistics urban–rural classification. “Large central metro” was renamed to “Urban”, “Large fringe metro” to “Suburban”, “Micropolitan” to “Small towns” and “Noncore” was renamed “Rural” in this graphic. Sources: US Census; NCHS Urban-Rural Classification Scheme; Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 district); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 district) Pearson said he was concerned that some voters were confused about which district they were in and that this could hurt turnout. Pearson’s advocacy for criminal justice reform and affordability has appealed to younger Democratic Party voters like 27-year-old Marko Jankov. But Jankov, who identifies as a Democratic Socialist, lives in a part of Memphis that was moved out of the 9th District and he said he was less motivated to vote for other Democrats when polls showed them unlikely to win. “They want to make it a psychological thing, where you think you can’t win,” Jankov said. The changes are exposing a rural-urban divide. Debby Gould, president of the non-partisan League of Women Voters of Tennessee, said voters of all backgrounds had concerns. “This is a time when we really have to strengthen urban-rural links and to come up with shared values,” she said. “Because rural voters are also feeling left out on this.” Hickey, the Williamson County Republican chair, said it was up to candidates to show they could work for all their constituents: “They’re going to have to put a lot of miles in their car.” Opening photo Elzey Avenue in Memphis, a dividing line between Congressional District 9 and Congressional District 5, following a Republican-led effort to redistrict Memphis. REUTERS/Seth Herald Sources US Census Bureau (2020 Census redistricting data, TIGER/Line); Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 congressional districts); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 congressional districts); State of Tennessee and the City of Memphis Engineering Division (city limits); Tennessee Department of Transportation (roads). Additional contributions by Travis Hartman, Ben Kellerman and Tiana McGee Edited by Claudia Parsons, Kat Stafford and Julia Wolfe More from Reuters Graphics

item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: Appetite for disruption
item.description: What connects Elon Musk’s flawed assault on US government waste with the latest attacks on Riyadh Airport? Both are a reminder of the importance of a functioning state, and the risks of economic upheaval. Plus: the financial fallout in the Gulf, and praise for messy economics.
item.dc:creator: Peter Thal Larsen
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! A week ago I [USN:L6N45V0TR TEXT:"highlighted"] some of the cracks in the foundations of the AI boom. Those fractures have widened as debt investors fret about [USN:L6N4610VQ TEXT:"neocloud data centre operators"] and Anthropic reports [USN:L6N4610VE TEXT:"slowing revenue growth"]. Temporary wobble or turning point? Email me with your views. If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend. OPENING LINE “The US commute is becoming an antique roadshow. Squeezed by high vehicle prices and borrowing costs, drivers are buying older cars with loans that last as long as eight years.” Read more: [USN:L6N44G18H TEXT:"The $1.7 trln auto loan market heads for a crash"] FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK The average price of an Anthropic token has dropped 68% since the start of 2025. ([USN:L6N4610VE TEXT:"The AI deflation trap"]) JPMorgan (JPM.N) added just $50 million to its allowance for consumer loan losses in the third quarter. ([USN:L6N45Z0W9 TEXT:"Jamie Dimon remains gloomy"]) Mukesh Ambani’s $102 billion Jio Platforms is set to go public on about the same valuation as rival telco Bharti Airtel (BRTI.NS) . ([USN:L6N45X01T TEXT:"IPO still makes sense"]) Qatar’s GDP is set to shrink by 16% this year. ([USN:L6N4600PN TEXT:"But rebound in 2027"]) Dating app Bumble has a quarter fewer paying users than in 2024. ([USN:L6N45Z0WC TEXT:"AI to the rescue?"]) CREATIVE OBSTRUCTION In the US government they are known as bus people. These are the low-key functionaries on whom the state depends. “Bus people are people who if they are hit by a bus the government stops working,” a political operative states in Michael Lewis’s new book. Civil servants are the unlikely heroes of “ Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State ”, the author’s inside account of the assault on US bureaucracy by Donald Trump’s second administration and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. The tale is something of a departure for Lewis, who has previously tended to favour plucky underdogs taking on an entrenched consensus. Think of the sceptical fund managers of “The Big Short”, or the data-obsessed baseball administrators of “Moneyball”. A decade ago, Lewis might have been more sympathetic to the ignorant laptop-wielding twentysomethings dispatched by Musk to root out waste and inefficiency in the US bureaucracy. Instead, the short-lived DOGE debacle has helped draw a definitive line under a three-decade celebration of disruption as a positive force. The word used to have mainly negative connotations. Then the tech revolutionaries of Silicon Valley grabbed the public imagination. Harvard professor Clayton Christensen lauded the power of disruption in his 1997 book “ The Innovator’s Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail ”. Suddenly, everyone with a smartphone could be a business revolutionary. Technological evangelists preached the benefits of applying the same approach to the core functions of the state: education, healthcare, defence and so on. Looking back, the surprise is how little resistance they faced. Even the 2008 financial crisis, which exposed the extreme fragility of modern banking, only encouraged more reckless experimentation with cryptocurrencies. It took a global pandemic, a trade conflict, and the knock-on effects from actual wars in Ukraine and Iran to remind many citizens of the importance of basic administrative competence. At the same time, Silicon Valley revealed its reckless instincts, which are now on daily display with each leap forward in artificial intelligence. Consumers might welcome AI agents that help them [USN:L6N45N158 TEXT:"find cheap flights"], but are unlikely to tolerate rogue bots filing false homicide tips with Philadelphia police, as Anthropic [USN:L8N45V1NQ TEXT:"admitted last week"]. Back in 2016, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman [USN:L8N19F4MY TEXT:"put on jeans and visited California"] to show his determination to modernise the kingdom. Business leaders praised his disruptive vision. Yet it’s hard to attract $100 billion a year of overseas investment when Houthi insurgents are [USN:L6N45Y0GN TEXT:"blowing up Riyadh’s main airport"]. Even executives who shrugged off the killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi will avoid the Saudi capital when their own safety is in doubt. This does not mean the government is necessarily efficient. Large sovereign debts and rising interest rates give politicians a strong impulse to seek more savings. The waves of “creative destruction” that Joseph Schumpeter described back in 1942 remain a feature of capitalist economies. Yet that system also depends on the state continuing to perform a wide range of everyday functions. It’s time we spent less of our attention on the self-professed disruptors, and more of it celebrating the bus people. CHART OF THE WEEK The latest war in the Gulf is doing serious economic damage. The leading economies in the Middle East are all set to shrink this year. The hope is that a peace deal will allow for a big bounce in 2027 as oil shipments resume and tourists return. Yet a prolonged conflict could undermine the region’s plans to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, write [USN:L6N4600PN TEXT:"George Hay and Afiq Fitri Alias"]. Meanwhile, the gusher of investment cash is dwindling as current account surpluses shrink. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS Did you know that almost all our data zips around the world on 600 fibre-optic cables laid on the ocean floor, most of them no wider than a garden hose? Neither did I until I read Katja Bego’s “Deep Connections: The Hidden Battles to Control Subsea Cables”, a new book about this fragile underwater network. On The Big View we discussed how subsea cables evolved, how they have been weaponised in the past, and whether the modern global network can survive rising geopolitical tensions. Imported Chinese cars are the current focus of trade tensions with the European Union. Aimee Donnellan beamed into the Viewsroom from the Paris Motor Show this week to debate the cap on Chinese imports – and whether European carmakers can survive the onslaught – with Antony Currie and Katrina Hamlin. PARTING SHOT The main surprise about this year’s Nobel Prize in Economics was that the winners did not already have one. Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were instrumental in reconciling the two main schools of the dismal science into what became known as the New Neoclassical Synthesis. This paved the way for the distillation of major economic problems into three equations, and the proliferation of models which remain influential today. Yet theoretical elegance came at the expense of practical utility, [USN:L6N45Y0MG TEXT:"argues Jon Sindreu"]. Today, a messier approach probably allows for better policymaking. item.title: Hargeisa like a local
item.description: Our digital journalist’s guide to camel milk tea, bustling markets and mobile money.
item.dc:creator: Hani Richter
item.content:encoded: REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans “Resilience is victory,” goes a famous Somali proverb, and few places embody it like Hargeisa. Turned to rubble by intense bombings during a decade-long war with Somalia, this Somaliland city was rebuilt through domestic grit and community labour. Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991, is my home away from home. It is where my mother spent her early childhood and where some of my extended family still live. Though I was born in Bonn, Germany, and grew up in London, where I joined Reuters as a social media editor in 2019, I have regularly visited Hargeisa. Every time, I wish I had stayed longer. Hargeisa translates as “the place where hides are sold” in Somali, and livestock remains the backbone of the economy, alongside remittances. But it is also a city where old meets new: People buy and sell lambs and goats through their phones, using mobile money to pay for food, clothing and much else. Here’s how to experience Hargeisa like a local: Getting around: Somaliland is a devoutly Muslim place where days start early, with the first call to prayer before sunrise acting as a natural alarm for many residents. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. Everyone is in a rush, so be aware of your surroundings and be mindful of manoeuvring cars, buses, motorbikes and even the occasional determined man with a wheelbarrow. People shop at an open-air market along a street in Hargeisa, Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in the Freedom Square along Independence Avenue. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader pours camel milk at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader handles camel milk from a steel can at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man stands next to second-hand clothes for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traders wait for customers as they sell second-hand clothes. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman waits for customers at her open-air butchery. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader displays mobile phones for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Vehicles parked outside Durdur Business Center, along Road No 1, 26 June District. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman uses her mobile phone as she walks past the New Moon restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man uses a sewing machine at his tailoring stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Shoes are displayed for sale at the Kaboole fashion store. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man sits inside the Muddakar coffee house restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman sells fruit at an open-air grocery stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit at a coffee shop. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traffic along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed For a more local experience, take a minibus. It’s a hail and ride system, so just flag down the bus as you would a taxi, confirm it’s going to your destination, and let the driver know when you want to get off. Note that they can often be crowded. For journeys outside of the centre, take a taxi or Dhaweeye, which translates as “closer” in English. They are always nearby and easily flagged off the street. Mobile money is king: As is the case in many African cities, mobile money is the preferred payment method in Hargeisa and to pay for anything you will need your phone. You don't need internet access; just ask which code to use and for the vendor's number. You can also pay with cash, of course, but it may take a bit longer. What to eat and drink: Many people make a living by selling their wares on the street. As you walk around the city, you will be called into restaurants and street stalls, where fruit sellers pile watermelons as tall as a person, and vendors fry potatoes. Camel meat and camel milk are must-tries. Somalis have been eating camel for centuries, a tradition rooted in the land’s arid landscape. When crops and cattle perished, camels were the only ones to survive. For a traditional snack on the go, try dried camel meat, called muqmaad. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. For breakfast , people enjoy stir-fried goat, lamb or beef liver with Somali pancakes (lahoox), or a flaky flatbread with honey that goes well with shaax, a spiced, aromatic tea made with camel milk that tastes very similar to chai. A favourite lunch is fragrant Somali rice (bariis) and meat, typically tender, bone-in goat or lamb — with a banana on the side. Tea is at the heart of social life in Hargeisa, and you will regularly see people sitting outside tea houses, drinking and talking politics. With Ethiopia next door, you are never far from a good cup of coffee either. Try Social Cafe, one of several cafes in the city or, for a Somali twist, order Qaxwo, made with spices such as ginger, cinnamon and cardamom. City landmarks: The Hargeisa War Memorial features a downed Somali Air Force MiG-17 aircraft. Located in Freedom Square, it is probably the city's most recognisable landmark. The livestock market offers a glimpse into one of the city's main economic drivers, and is particularly interesting if you have never experienced the pastoral side of Somali culture. You’ll see large numbers of goats, sheep and camels being sold. Go in the morning to see it at its busiest. If you are looking for entertainment, stop by the Hiddo Dhawr Cultural Centre. Founded in 2013 by Somali singer and activist Sahra Halgan, it often features live performances of Somali music and poetry. For an authentic shopping experience, visit the Waheen Market, the city's main commercial market, where you will find everything from mattresses and glassware to gold jewellery. It’s also a great place to pick up a souvenir. One popular option is a dhill, a traditional wooden vessel used to store milk, usually adorned with leather straps and cowrie shells. Another is frankincense, an aromatic resin. Somaliland is one of the few places in the world where frankincense grows naturally. The gum is chewed for its health benefits, while the resin is traditionally burned to freshen homes and welcome guests. Finally, no visit to Hargeisa is complete without a trip to the money market, a famous open-air street market where vendors trade bricks of local currency and US dollars. There are piles of cash as far as the eye can see — but with mobile money now the first choice, who knows how long it will be there. Dress like a local: Hargeisa is a conservative place where people dress modestly. To fit in, try sporting some traditional dress. Women wear beautiful dresses called baatis with matching hijabs, often in tie-dye or other intricate designs, while men wear a sarong wrap decorated with traditional prints. When to visit: If you are visiting during the summer months, when it is hottest, expect average temperatures of around 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit) during the day. In winter, temperatures reach about 26 C (79 F) at their highest, which is considered cool. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population : 1.3 million Price of a cup of tea : $0.20 to $1.50. My go-to spot for breakfast or lunch is CFC. Great place to watch the sunset : Sarovar Hotel is located at the top of a mountain and offers an unforgettable view of Hargeisa. Largest university : University of Hargeisa, more than 7,000 students

item.title: Chuck Lorre on his reign as the ‘King of Sitcoms’
item.description: The television writer and producer behind “The Big Bang Theory” and “Two and a Half Men” reflects on his career, the key to great comedy, and why he remains optimistic about television.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Serhan
item.content:encoded: American television producer Chuck Lorre poses for a portrait at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, US, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Cole Laughter, Chuck Lorre is keen to point out, is not a voluntary act. It is not something we choose, but something that happens to us, like an unexpected gift. Lorre knows something about making it happen. Dubbed the “King of Sitcoms,” he has spent decades making audiences laugh, from his early work as a writer on the hit comedy “Roseanne” to creating shows, including “The Big Bang Theory,” “Two and a Half Men,” “Mom,” and “Mike & Molly.” In his newly released memoir, “Sitcom,” Lorre turns that comic instinct on his own life, writing candidly about his missteps, while also looking back at the television successes and creative battles that shaped his career. Speaking with Reuters from Los Angeles, he discusses why character is key to great comedy, what he learned from getting things wrong, and why he’s optimistic about the TV industry’s future. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. The memoir is very funny despite tackling difficult subjects, from failed marriages to addiction and Scientology. What made you want to open up about them now? From the outset, I was trying to write it as if I was having a conversation with somebody. Rather than reporting or reiterating stuff, I was trying to write it as if I was talking to the audience or talking to a person; more conversational as opposed to you know, being locked up in the prose of it all. I've been talking about these crazy chapters of my life for a long time and dear friend nudged me for at least two years to start writing it down. And once I started writing it down, I was quite pleasantly surprised. I realized it was cathartic. It was it was a little bit of therapy for me. Having finished the darned thing, what became really clear was all the missteps I've made in my life were all necessary for me to arrive at where I am, and I am deeply grateful for where I am. So the path may have been bumpy, but that's what was required. What most excites you about television right now, and what terrifies you? There's plenty in this world that is terrifying, but I wouldn't put TV in that category. Actually, I'm an optimist about how the business is changing. I've heard people complain that there's too many choices. And to me that's like, really? Does that mean when you walk into a supermarket, you complain that there's too many choices? That's got to be a good thing. When I came up in this in television, there was three and a half networks. Fox was just starting. And that was it. If those three said no, it's simply not going to happen. Now there's I don't know how many platforms capable of helping a writer (or) performer create something and perhaps get it seen by a legitimate audience. Of all the shows you’ve created, which felt most miraculous? Probably Big Bang. I mean, the first pilot was an abject failure, with the exception of (co-stars) Johnny Galecki and Jim Parsons. I had to wrap my head around the fact that it was poorly written and, when we were given another opportunity one year later, we got a chance to write a better pilot. You don't get do-overs in this business, but we did. Actress Kaley Cuoco along with the cast and writers of "Big Bang Theory" accept their award for favorite TV comedy at the 2010 People's Choice Awards in Los Angeles January 6, 2010. REUTERS/Lucy Nicholson I didn't understand what we were creating till we created it. I didn't understand how viscerally the audience was going to connect with these outliers, these brilliant but incompetent characters. What makes a great comedy? It's really very simple. It's about characters. Well-designed, thought out characters, portrayed by the right actor. I adored "Cheers" and "Seinfeld" and "Everybody Loves Raymond," "Archie Bunker," Norman Lear's stuff. I wasn't watching for the plot. The storytelling of it was secondary. It was these extraordinary characters that I loved and I wanted to see them every week. And that's how I've always approached creating television shows. Character, character, character. I don't think I could sit here and remember one storyline for "Cheers," but I never missed an episode because I wanted to see those characters. Those characters made me laugh. And I think that's the secret sauce for comedy. Obviously, when you work in the drama world, plotting is an entirely different thing. You're watching for the adventure, the hero's journey. That's a story. But even in that world, which I know very little about, I'm thinking about character. Going back to the importance of casting, you write about the resistance you faced casting Melissa McCarthy in “Mike & Molly,” with one network executive pushing for a slimmer actress. How much has the industry changed, and how did you learn which battles were worth fighting? The nominees for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series (L-R) Martha Plimpton, Melissa McCarthy, Amy Poehler and Edie Faco stand on stage as they congratulate winner McCarthy from "Mike & Molly" at the 63rd Primetime Emmy Awards in Los Angeles September 18, 2011. REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni Well, the good news is, because I've had some success, I don't have that many battles anymore. But it took a long time for me to fight for who I believed in as opposed to being a good soldier and taking direction. I learned the hard way that when you do what you're told to do by others and you fail, it's your failure. It's not theirs. At a certain point, I started to dig my heels in and I think first and most formidably (was) with Jon Cryer. I talk about how much resistance I got from CBS to cast Jon in "Two and a Half Men" and then Melissa McCarthy. Here was a generational talent and it was "over my dead body" kind of casting. And I went, "Fine, well, produce a dead body because we're going over it." I guess what I'm trying to say is, it took me a while to find the courage to fight these fights. I didn't have it in the beginning. I was too frightened about being tossed aside and sent home. American television producer Chuck Lorre poses for a portrait at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, US, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Cole How concerned are you about AI in the writers’ room? Are the protections won in the 2023 writers’ strike enough? There's plenty of reason to be concerned about this technology. Television would be the least of it, I would think. Why is that? I just think, if we're going to prioritize our concerns, for me AI is concerning in that it could topple civilization, not take away jobs on sitcoms, not that that's not important. But creating an intelligence that so wildly surpasses human intelligence is an incredibly risky endeavor. Look what we've done as the apex predator on this planet. Imagine what would happen if there was an apex-apex predator that viewed us the way we view insects. That scares me. Do you expect to see more shows tapping into those fears? We did an episode on "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" with an AI overlord that has shock collars around everyone so when they get angry or contentious and asocial, they're shocked into submission. You write that good TV writing starts with reading good writing. What happens to television if people are reading less? I really love words. I love the meaning of words, the sound of words, the music of words. And comedy, from my perspective, is really absolutely correct use of words to cause a response; to cause laughter. And laughter happens to you. Real laughter is involuntary. It should surprise the laugher. And that's a result of both words and images. I guess I could be concerned about a future where words become less relevant because they're my favorite things. Finally, some quick-fire questions. If you had to cast someone to portray you, who would you insist on? Idris Elba. No? Maybe not. (laughs) Why would you even ask that question? Are we going to make a movie out of the book? You never know! If you could revisit one of your shows, which would it be? "Dharma and Greg." I've always felt a profound regret for having left. There was so much more to explore, but I didn't know how. What’s your comfort watch? I really am drawn to dramas. I like to watch what I don't do. I love "Slow Horses" and "Furious." "Lucky" was another thing I saw and really enjoyed. "The Diplomat" is (also) terrific. As far as current comedies are concerned, if I want to laugh, I watch John Oliver and Jon Stewart. They absolutely know how to make me laugh out loud. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital
item.description: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon. Le souverain pontife, âgé de 71 ans, s'est rendu sans aide jusqu'à la voiture qui l'attendait, s'arrêtant pour saluer les fidèles rassemblés devant l'hôpital Gemelli de Rome. Ses médecins avaient précédemment indiqué qu'il se sentait suffisamment bien pour rentrer chez lui après avoir effectué les dernières analyses sanguines et examens d'imagerie thoracique. Le pape, qui a subi mardi une opération visant à lui retirer le lobe inférieur du poumon droit, fera dimanche sa première apparition publique depuis son intervention pour prononcer la traditionnelle prière de l'Angélus sur la place Saint-Pierre, a confirmé le Saint-Siège. Léon a reçu un diagnostic d’adénocarcinome pulmonaire, la forme la plus courante de cancer du poumon. Ce diagnostic, pour un pape connu pour être relativement jeune et énergique et qui n’a été élu qu’en mai 2025, a provoqué un choc et soulevé des questions quant à l’avenir de son pontificat alors qu’il doit faire face à la maladie. Les médecins du pape ont indiqué que son opération s’était déroulée avec succès, sans complications. Ils n’ont toutefois pas encore révélé la taille de la tumeur ni précisé si la maladie s’était propagée aux ganglions lymphatiques voisins, deux facteurs essentiels pour établir le pronostic.

item.title: Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after cancer surgery
item.description: A smiling Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how his 17-month papacy might change.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: A smiling Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how his 17-month papacy might change. The pope walked unaided to his waiting car, waving to well-wishers outside Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He stopped to speak to a 13-year-old girl named Varvara from Ukraine who has been in Italy for cancer treatment. Leo, 71, was pictured smiling broadly and waving through an open window when his black SUV left the hospital grounds. He appeared in good spirits as he left the hospital in video released by the Vatican. He shook hands with a group of Franciscan friars, one of whom said: "This is the second time (we have met). Let's hope there will be a third and fourth." The pope laughed and replied: "Many times, but not for these reasons." PRAYERS ON SUNDAY His doctors had said earlier on Saturday that he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging, and that he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. Leo, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery when he will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims from his apartment overlooking St. Peter's Square at noon (1000 GMT) on Sunday. He has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"raised questions"] about the future shape of his papacy. The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis. SOUTH AMERICAN TRIP Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said that Leo could be fully recovered in another 10 days and that there was no reason to call off his planned visit to South America next month. "As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place," he told the Vatican News website. Leo is planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a pope [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"in decades"]. Margaritora said the tumour had been discovered by chance during what he called a routine abdominal examination. The Vatican signaled on Friday that Leo, known for following a busy schedule, intended to keep up his commitments, as some cardinals began to publicly express concern about the pope's health. In a sign the pope was back to work, Leo held a phone call on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, [USN:L8N4621IK TEXT:"urging a ceasefire"] to help get vital supplies into Oleshky, a Russian-controlled Ukrainian town. Lebanese pilgrim Abdul Halim Fatha was in St. Peter's Square as Leo arrived back at the Vatican and expressed sadness over the pope's cancer diagnosis. "But I know God will be with him and protect him," he said.

item.title: Indian state food safety authority names Reliance, Blinkit executives in expired food probe
item.description: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Chaturvedi
item.content:encoded: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters. The Food and Drug Administration of Maharashtra state, home to Mumbai, has led a [USN:L4N44Z0MR TEXT:"crackdown"] on food safety under its chief Tukaram Mundhe, 51, including shutting down some of Mumbai’s most popular eateries as well as outlets of Domino’s and Pizza Hut for poor hygiene. The state agency has also suspended the permit of a McDonald’s outlet. The latest case, which has led to a police complaint by the food safety authority, involves large retail and quick-commerce companies, which sell products to millions of households in the world’s most populous country. Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, according to the documents reviewed by Reuters, said its officials visited some warehouses of Reliance Retail, Reliance Consumer and Zomato Hyperpure, and that company officials could not provide verifiable proof that disposal of expired food was actually carried out by their contractors. "The disposal agencies ... do not destroy the stock," the case document alleged. In the case of a Zomato Hyperpure warehouse, a company representative named a contractor as its disposal agency which FDA officials could not trace, according to the documents. Reliance and Blinkit did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. "Any attempt to divert expired, damaged or consumer-rejected food products meant for destruction back into the market is a serious matter that demands strict scrutiny and accountability," Maharashtra's FDA chief Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters. "No company, brand, business or individual is above the law when it comes to food safety." INDIA'S INTENSIFYING CRACKDOWN Reliance Retail and Reliance Consumer are part of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s business group. Zomato’s Hyperpure is a unit of Eternal that also runs food delivery service Zomato and quick commerce business Blinkit. The FDA probe said it found a pattern where large retail and quick commerce distribution warehouses handed over expired and customer-rejected packages of food to contractors who passed the food to unlicensed sorting yards. These sorting yards then separated out saleable-looking packets, which eventually reached other retailers and the consumer market, according to case documents from the probe. "The chain thus runs from company warehouse to disposal agency, unlicensed yard, broker, retailer and consumer." The Maharashtra FDA on Thursday suspended the licences of five establishments in the state — three Reliance and two Eternal entities, the case documents said. Enforcement of food safety laws has traditionally been weak in India and the recent round of extensive crackdowns has garnered large-scale public support. In August, Indian authorities [USN:L4N44S18T TEXT:"raided"] an illegal operation in Mumbai that faked expiry dates and nutritional information on original food products manufactured by PepsiCo (PEP.O) , Nestle (NESN.S) , Coca-Cola (KO.N) and Unilever, so they could be exported to other countries. (This story has been corrected to say 'Reliance retail and consumer units,' not 'Reliance Group entities,' in paragraph 1.)

item.title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers
item.description: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
item.dc:creator: David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030. Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act. Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery. He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion". Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an [USN:L6N4611F6 TEXT:"initial public offering"] expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion. HUMANS IN CONTROL, FOR NOW Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control. "We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials. AI was a major topic at the IMF and World Bank meetings, as both a [USN:L1N45Z01U TEXT:"source of growth"] offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash. Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind. But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants. More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said. STRICTEST CONTROLS ON BIOLOGICAL RESEARCH Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology. "Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have many choices to make," he said. Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety." Despite some recent high-profile incidents where [USN:L4N45N1OZ TEXT:"rogue AI systems"] have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to impose safeguards was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years." Clark also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

item.title: India's HDFC Bank Q2 profit rises 4.7%; deputy MD Bharucha to step down
item.description: India's largest private-sector lender, HDFC Bank , reported a second-quarter profit on Saturday that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset strong lending growth.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: India's largest private-sector lender, HDFC Bank (HDBK.NS) , reported a second-quarter profit on Saturday that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset strong lending growth. The lender also said in a regulatory filing that its deputy managing director Kaizad Bharucha will step down at the end of December. The news comes days before a leadership change at the Mumbai-based lender. Anup Bagchi, a veteran of the ICICI group, takes over as managing director and CEO for three years from October 27, becoming HDFC Bank's first external chief executive. Bharucha, who has been with HDFC Bank for over three decades, was one of two contenders for the top job, Reuters had [USN:L4N44R00C TEXT:"reported"]. Bagchi [USN:L1N45N0I6 TEXT:"takes charge"] amid increased scrutiny of the bank's governance, profitability and operational performance. The lender posted a standalone net profit of 195.10 billion Indian rupees ($2.05 billion) for the quarter ended September 30, compared with 186.41 billion rupees a year earlier. Analysts had estimated a profit of 195.26 billion rupees, according to data compiled by LSEG. Treasury trading gains fell to 7.8 billion rupees from 23.9 billion rupees a year earlier, weighing on earnings despite broad-based loan growth. Other income, which includes gains on bonds and other investments, fell 3.6% to 138.31 billion rupees. Indian lenders reported strong credit growth in the quarter across corporate and retail loans. HDFC Bank's net interest income rose 9.7% to 346.19 billion rupees, with total loans up 16.3%. Deposits grew 18.8% from a year earlier, and the credit-to-deposit ratio stood at 96.0%. Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies rose 2.1% to 35.74 billion rupees. Asset quality improved. The gross non-performing asset ratio was 1.11% at the end of September, compared with 1.17% at the end of June. ($1 = 94.9600 Indian rupees)

item.title: Un ministre russe au FMI boycotté par les Européens
item.description: Plusieurs délégués du comité de pilotage du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) ont quitté samedi une réunion au moment où le ministre russe des Finances, Anton Silouanov, prenait la parole, rapportent trois sources présentes.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Plusieurs délégués du comité de pilotage du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) ont quitté samedi une réunion au moment où le ministre russe des Finances, Anton Silouanov, prenait la parole, rapportent trois sources présentes. "De nombreuses délégations ont quitté les lieux, dont des membres de l'Union européenne", a dit l'une des sources. Selon une deuxième source, une dizaine de délégués dont ceux du Danemark, de la Suède, de la Finlande, de la Norvège et des pays baltes ont quitté la pièce où se déroulait la réunion. "La guerre en Ukraine est existentielle pour nous en Europe", a déclaré un diplomate européen. "Nous ne pouvons pas normaliser nos relations avec la Russie." Jeudi, l'Allemagne a mis en garde contre les efforts visant à réintégrer la Russie au sein d'institutions internationales, après la participation d'Anton Silouanov à une réunion des ministres des Finances et banquiers centraux du G20 à Asheville, en Caroline du Nord, à la fin août. Les Etats-Unis, qui président pour l'heure le G20, avaient soutenu la présence du ministre russe en dépit de l'opposition des Européens. "Je constate des tentatives, notamment de la part des États-Unis (...) visant à ramener la Russie sur la scène internationale", a déclaré jeudi aux journalistes Lars Klingbeil, le ministre allemand des Finances. "Il est hors de question de faire comme si la Russie redevenait un membre normal du G20 et reprenait tout simplement sa place à la table, en tout cas, pas avec moi, ni avec les autres Européens." Les dirigeants de l'UE ont affiché vendredi, lors de leur sommet à Bruxelles, leur soutien au président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky, objet depuis plusieurs jours de vives critiques de son homologue américain Donald Trump. Le locataire de la Maison blanche a conclu un accord la semaine dernière avec Moscou pour autoriser l'exportation de diesel russe et annoncé vendredi la levée de plusieurs sanctions, restrictions et droits de douane visant la Russie pourtant prévus dans le cadre d'une loi votée par le Congrès qu'il avait promulguée le mois dernier.

item.title: Rennie promises All Blacks will stick to their guns at World Cup
item.description: New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said his team would be sticking to their expansive style at next year's World Cup after the All Blacks thrashed the Wallabies for a second successive week with some sensational attacking rugby on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Nick Mulvenney
item.content:encoded: New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said his team would be sticking to their expansive style at next year's World Cup after the All Blacks thrashed the Wallabies for a second successive week with some sensational attacking rugby on Saturday. Two convincing wins over Australia have got the three-times world champions back to winning ways after they lost a four-match series against South Africa 3-1. The Springboks have ridden a physical, conservative playing style to back-to-back World Cup triumphs but Rennie said he remained convinced the tactics that put a premium on ball speed and width would be effective against it. "There's no point playing this way and then going to a World Cup and trying to play risk-free footy," he told reporters after the 42-21 victory at Stadium Australia. "We're well aware you can put yourself under pressure the way that we're trying to play, but we'll also back ourselves that we'll profit more than we'll suffer in those situations. "I don't think you want all the teams in the world playing the same game. I think if you look at the Wallabies, they're pretty similar to us. I think they'll want to play, and it's a point of difference, part of the DNA of both sides." "If you want to just get into arm wrestles with a couple of the big sides in the world, it'll be a struggle," he said. Despite his team scoring six tries with some breathtaking rugby in the first half on Saturday, Rennie said there were still improvements to be made. "We're trying to grow our game, and we've got a long way to go," he said. "We just want to be able to play at a tempo that will test other sides." Australia coach Les Kiss said he was pleased with the performance of flyhalf Declan Meredith in only his fourth test and remained confident the Wallabies could put on a good showing at their home World Cup next year. "I've always said we'll have ups and downs, and today it was a bit of a downer again," he said. "But there are some good clues about what we're trying to do in our game. When we do play with footy in the hand with a positive intent, we're making a lot of breaks against one of the best teams in the world. "So I think there are some good qualities that are coming through. So I'm optimistic still."
