item.title: Tanker struck by unknown projectile off Saudi Arabia on Friday, UKMTO says
item.description: An unknown projectile struck a tanker 68 nautical miles northeast of Saudi Arabia's Jubail on Friday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in a report on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An unknown projectile struck a tanker 68 nautical miles northeast of Saudi Arabia's Jubail on Friday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in a report on Saturday. All crew members were safe and had been evacuated, it said, adding that no environmental impact had been reported. UKMTO later issued a second report on Saturday that a tanker was attacked by a rocket-propelled grenade from a small boat 78 nautical miles northeast of Jubail on Friday, damaging its aft port quarter. All crew members were safe, it said, while the full extent of the damage and the environmental impact was not yet known. Reuters could not immediately establish whether the two reports referred to the same incident.

item.title: Russia says it hit Ukrainian steel plants, power infrastructure and ships
item.description: Russia said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian and infrastructure targets including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih, and vessels using the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian and infrastructure targets including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih, and vessels using the Ukrainian port of Odesa. The plant is owned by steel giant ArcelorMittal , which [USN:L1N45H03O TEXT:"suspended"] operations there in September after a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement, Russia's defence ministry said the plant supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex. It said Russian forces had also hit an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr and another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line. A cargo vessel in the Black Sea was also hit, the ministry said, alleging that it was delivering military cargo to Odesa. Later in the day, the ministry said Russian strikes during the afternoon had hit a vehicle-repair plant in Lutsk, an electricity substation in the western Ternopil region and another cargo vessel south of Odesa that it said was carrying military and dual-use cargo. Reuters could not independently confirm the ministry's reports.

item.title: India's Axis Bank quarterly profit rises 37.6%, but misses estimates on higher costs
item.description: Indian private-sector lender Axis Bank reported on Saturday a quarterly profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as higher operating expenses and weaker other income offset robust credit growth and lower provisions.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: Indian private-sector lender Axis Bank (AXBK.NS) reported on Saturday a quarterly profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as higher operating expenses and weaker other income offset robust credit growth and lower provisions. Axis Bank, the country's third-largest private bank by assets, posted a stand-alone net profit of 70.03 billion Indian rupees ($737.5 million) for the quarter ended on September 30, compared with 50.90 billion rupees a year earlier. Analysts, on average, had forecast a profit of 71.24 billion rupees, according to LSEG-compiled data. Other income, which includes earnings from bonds and other investments, fell 1.4% to 65.31 billion rupees. Rising bond yields and volatility in the rupee during the quarter weighed on treasury income at the Mumbai-based lender, tempering earnings even as lending expanded across segments. Banks across India reported strong loan growth during the quarter across corporate and retail portfolios. Net interest income grew 11.8% to 153.71 billion rupees, helped by a 23% rise in total loans. Deposits increased 20.7% from a year earlier. Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies fell 52.2% to 16.94 billion rupees. The gross non-performing asset ratio stood at 1.16% at end-September, compared with 1.28% three months earlier. ($1 = 94.9600 Indian rupees)

item.title: ECB's Lagarde says bond selloff will slow inflation
item.description: A selloff in bonds is making borrowing more expensive in the euro zone, curbing economic growth and ultimately inflation, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Canepa
item.content:encoded: A selloff in bonds is making borrowing more expensive in the euro zone, curbing economic growth and ultimately inflation, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde said on Saturday. Bond yields around the world have surged in recent weeks, with [USN:L1N46002V TEXT:"debt-laden France"] among the hardest hit, on the back of worries about debt and inflation as well as growing [USN:L1N4620D1 TEXT:"competition for credit"] from AI investments. Lagarde said this would make it harder than the ECB had projected last month for consumers to absorb higher fuel prices from the Iran war. "While growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting," Lagarde told fellow central bankers and finance ministers gathering in Bangkok. "This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise." The ECB has raised interested rates twice in the last four months and a further hike is expected in December, which would take its policy rate to 2.75% — a level it considers restrictive, or curtailing economic activity. Fellow ECB policymaker Joachin Nagel hinted at more policy tightening ahead, although he added that the central bank would decide at each meeting based on incoming data. "We are fighting against inflation, I'm of the opinion that the job is not done so far," the Bundesbank president told a DZ Bank event in the Thai capital. "I do see that maybe we have to do more." Speaking alongside Nagel, his Finnish colleague Olli Rehn said the ECB would watch out for "second-round effects" from energy inflation on other prices and wages. "There is no sign of second-round effects, but we will stay vigilant because they might creep in quietly like a cat in socks," Rehn said.

item.title: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
item.description: A young lawmaker demands as new future as protests rage in Tirana.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Marjana Koceku's life changed last year when Prime Minister Edi Rama hand-picked her to run for Albania's parliament, one of a legion of young lawmakers he hoped would become the face of his Socialist Party. This week, however, the 25-year-old, now an independent member of parliament, joined [USN:L1N4610AQ TEXT:"mass student protests"] calling for Rama to step down. Corruption, a lack of jobs and a general feeling that the government does not work for them have created a deep-seated anger that spilled over this week, when young protesters swarmed the capital Tirana, setting fire to government buildings and banks and hurling pavement stones at police. The government and the police have condemned the violence. According to police figures, 500 protestors have been detained, 330 of whom have been released. Some 120 police and 45 protesters have been injured, the figures show, although the protester figure is likely higher given that many injuries have gone unrecorded. Albania's unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe, including in France, where high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities. YOUTH PROTESTS THREATEN RAMA'S RULE "The country is amazing, but ... the wrong policies that have been implemented by this political elite are completely against what the Albanian communities and Albanian citizens have been asking and seeking for so long," Koceku said during the protests on Friday as police fired tear gas and water cannon at protesters nearby. Rama, a former basketball player, has been in power since 2013, half Koceku's life. He won a fourth term in elections last year but his administration has since been dogged by corruption scandals. Rama denies wrongdoing and this week told Reuters that he would not step down. "Governments are changed through democratic elections and we had them last year, not through violence," he said. Still, the protests represent the biggest threat to his rule yet. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania's pristine southern coastline. The project, whose backers include US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has faced legal challenges. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"wrongfully sold"] for the development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was [USN:L6N4380FB TEXT:"wanted by prosecutors"] on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. He did not respond to requests for comment. That was not the only controversy for Rama's government. Last year, prosecutors alleged that his deputy prime minister was involved in [USN:L6N3ZC0BA TEXT:"doling out construction contracts"] to favoured companies, charges Rama and the deputy deny. "I didn't agree, especially with the policies that they were implementing against nature, and our land and our Albania," Koceku said. This week, protesters said they had resorted to violence because they had not felt heard. The Kushner-backed project upset Koceku, who has a close relationship with the land. She is from the remote mountains of northern Albania where her family runs a small, no-frills guest house on the shore of a lake. "Our country is the Albanian people," she said, the air around her thick with acrid tear gas. "They create the future, they create the now, and they are the ones who can bring our country forward. Not a single person, not a single government."

item.title: China AI supply-chain IPOs hold firm despite valuation pullback, Citi says
item.description: Listings of Chinese AI supply chain companies are expected to stand their ground weathering rising valuation concerns and increasingly sharper scrutiny, a Citi banker working with Chinese companies said.
item.dc:creator: Selena Li
item.content:encoded: Listings of Chinese AI supply chain companies are expected to stand their ground weathering rising valuation concerns and increasingly sharper scrutiny, a Citi (C.N) banker working with Chinese companies said. Despite recent [USN:L1N46118D TEXT:"valuation"] pullbacks on data centre companies, largely originating from the US market, future AI supply-chain listings would continue in Hong Kong, said Simon Yuan, Citi's head of China investment banking. Chinese companies plan to list in Hong Kong are cushioned by a roughly even split between domestic Chinese and international demand, Yuan, who also heads Citi’s financial institutions group in APAC, said on the sidelines of the IMF meetings in Bangkok. The market is supported by a pool of local liquidity, with rising southbound capital from the Chinese mainland emerging as a key buying force, Yuan said. Still, "if the whole AI cycle turns in the US — and we have seen some volatility in the last few weeks — you will see an impact everywhere, Hong Kong included,” he warned. Many Chinese hardware players have proactively established manufacturing footprints outside mainland China, he said, which helps them better service global clients and mitigate geopolitical friction. Chinese hardware suppliers have benefited from the global AI infrastructure boom, gaining both sales volume growth and higher unit prices, Yuan said. Next year, the focus in Hong Kong's equity capital markets is expected to shift away from pure hardware, toward Chinese artificial intelligence models and application developers, he said. "But these companies need to have a proven business model. They need to show very strong growth and profitability," he said. Propelled by Chinese tech funding demand, 118 firms went public in Hong Kong in the first nine months of the year, raising HK$388 billion ($49.4 billion), up 106% year-on-year. ($1 = 7.8479 Hong Kong dollars) (This story has been corrected to say 'Yuan', not 'Yuen', throughout.)

item.title: IMF members call for more support amid war shocks, 'advanced intelligence' risks
item.description: International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside.
item.dc:creator: David Lawder
item.content:encoded: International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside. And while there has been a boost to investment and trade from "advanced intelligence technologies", they also carried risks, the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee said in a statement after a meeting in Bangkok. "Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security," said the statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chair of the IMFC. The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender. Al-Jadaan told Reuters that the language of the statement was agreed by all members. Earlier this week, the United States was pressing fellow IMF members to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" in the statement, in line with US President Donald Trump's preferred name for the technology, a [USN:L1N4610GV TEXT:"senior US Treasury official told Reuters"]. The final version of the chair's statement contained no reference to artificial intelligence. It said the uncertain impact of "advanced intelligence technologies", along with rising bond yields in major economies that spill over to highly indebted economies, "could amplify macro-financial vulnerabilities." "Rapid technological change, demographic shifts, more frequent extreme weather events and natural disasters, and geoeconomic fragmentation are compounding policy tradeoffs," the statement said. The member economies agreed to support countries that undertake reforms and address debt vulnerabilities, with specific attention to low-income and vulnerable middle-income countries and conflict-affected states. "We encourage increasing support to countries with sustainable debt and strong reform and growth enhancing agenda, but facing short-term financing challenges," the statement said, noting that several members had provided assurances of support to the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which supports poor and developing countries.

item.title: Strong dollar, weak hand for Trump before midterms
item.description: A surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: With the US midterm elections weeks away, a surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Donald Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants. Trump's economic record in the first two years of his second term is being heavily scrutinized. Polls show voters' approval of his handling of the economy has rarely been lower. That goes a long way toward explaining why [USN:L4N45Y17K TEXT:"betting markets "]point to his Republican Party losing control of the House of Representatives, and perhaps even the Senate, on November 3. Yet if there's any truth to the market adage that a country's currency is a reflection of the world's confidence in its economy, Trump should be going into the upcoming vote brimming with confidence. The dollar (.DXY) has been rising steadily, recently hitting its [USN:L4N46001K TEXT:"strongest level in 18 months"] against major peers. But a strong and appreciating exchange rate is the last thing Trump wants. His administration's economic and trade policies are aiming to revive US manufacturing, make American exports great again and shrink the trade deficit. A strengthening currency won't help with any of that. WRONG DIRECTION One might expect the dollar to be under pressure, especially given that the [USN:L1N45R0RR TEXT:"US trade balance"] has not narrowed according to the administration's plan. Imports have exploded to record levels, largely driven by US companies hoovering up the chips, equipment and goods needed for the AI build-out , and the country's trade deficit is widening. It was [USN:L1N45F0L5 TEXT:"2.7% of gross domestic product"] earlier this year — one of the smallest readings of the century — but it could be headed for 4% of GDP next year, according to Dean Maki at hedge fund Point72. But the dollar is not weakening. It did during Trump's first year back in the Oval Office, amid concerns about [USN:L1N44H0RB TEXT:""dollar debasement""] and a "sell America" mentality among foreign investors fostered by Trump's tariffs , but that has since gone into reverse. Why? Because exchange rates are relative, and the greenback currently appears to be the proverbial "cleanest dirty shirt." While the US is suffering from acute debt and deficit concerns, so are other developed countries, most [USN:S8N50E09F TEXT:"notably France"]. Investors fear that Paris is unwilling to take the politically unpalatable steps to get its budget under control and are thus slamming the euro . Similarly, worries that higher interest rates will make it nearly impossible for Japan to service its [USN:SPN45900X TEXT:"enormous debt load"] have anchored the yen near its recent historical lows. In short, the dollar is "winning" as much by default as it is benefiting from the flood of global capital chasing the US AI dream. This is not what the White House had in mind. Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent clearly [USN:L8N3YR24M TEXT:"want a weaker dollar"], even if decades of a quasi-official "strong dollar" policy at the White House — dating back to the days of former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin in the 1990s — make it challenging for them to say so outright. The Trump administration's views on the US currency were flagged almost exactly two years ago in "A User’s Guide to Restructuring the Global Trading System," a paper by Stephen Miran, then a senior strategist at hedge fund Hudson Bay Capital Management. Miran went on to serve as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Trump, who later appointed him as a Federal Reserve governor for a short spell. He has since returned to HBC, but his 41-page manual still appears to serve as a broad framework for the administration's trade, currency and economic policy. The blueprint has come to be known as the "Mar-a-Lago Accord," in a nod to the famous 1985 "Plaza Accord," under which the world's leading economic powers agreed to devalue the dollar. Echoing Trump's decades-long view, Miran wrote that "deep unhappiness with the prevailing economic order is rooted in persistent overvaluation of the dollar ... (which) makes US exports less competitive, US imports cheaper, and handicaps American manufacturing." He has a point. At the time of Trump's inauguration in January last year, the dollar's broad, real effective exchange rate was the strongest in over 30 years. Miran argues that the global trade and financial systems can be rewired to America's benefit, but the path "is narrow, and will require careful planning, precise execution, and attention to steps to minimize adverse consequences." Americans casting their midterm election votes on November 3 may not have the patience for this. While the US economy continues to grow at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, households are feeling the adverse economic consequences of Trump's policies over the past two years. Tariffs have raised the cost of imported goods, according to a recent New York Fed study , and the US war with Iran, launched in February, has led to soaring energy costs, most notably record-high diesel prices at the pump. As a consequence, inflation remains elevated, bond yields are the highest in a quarter of a century, and real wages are now falling. Given all this, the big question is whether the American public will give the Trump administration the space to try to turn the dollar's tide. A FAREWELL TO MULTILATERALISM Efforts to reverse the dollar's march higher will be challenging, to put it mildly. History suggests that what's needed is multilateral, globally coordinated action, but that is the antithesis of Trump's "America First" worldview. Piecemeal and bilateral actions, like the Treasury's recent [USN:L4N45304A TEXT:"intervention with Japan"] to support the yen , are likely too small to have any lasting impact. Further interventions cannot be ruled out if the dollar continues to strengthen. For example, when writing about the yen, Stephen Jen, CEO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management, recently argued that a series of targeted, surprise "mini" interventions could chip away at the dollar without triggering an avalanche of depreciation, helping the Trump administration meet its foreign exchange and wider goals over time. "The Trump Administration ... wants to find ways to guide the dollar lower. This is needed because, in order for the US to attain economic security, it needs to reclaim a certain level of manufacturing self-sufficiency. To do that, a weaker dollar would be necessary. The challenge, of course, is to guide the dollar lower without spooking the capital markets," Jen wrote in May. Much will depend on the frequency and size of such moves. Official action to weaken the dollar against major currencies is rare. Before this year's yen intervention, the last time US and Japanese authorities coordinated to sell dollars against the yen was in 1998. The Fed intervened with the European Central Bank and other authorities to support the euro, but that was back in late 2000, just after the single currency's launch. Since the era of free-floating exchange rates began in the early 1970s, when President Richard Nixon took the US off the gold standard, there have only been two truly global efforts to force a change in the dollar's broad value. Both were in the 1980s: the Plaza Accord in 1985 to lower what was an extremely elevated dollar, and the Louvre Accord in 1987 to essentially take the sting out of Plaza. These accords were products of their time. The dollar is nowhere near as strong as it was back then, and that was an era when multilateral cooperation was still in vogue. As the country looks set to enter the final two years of the Trump era, the dollar's relative strength could say much about how much of his economic agenda he has been able to achieve since first entering the White House almost 10 years ago. item.title: IMFC chair says global economy resilient; delegates walk out on Russian official
item.description: A US official said Washington supports Russia's presence despite European concerns.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal, David Lawder, Jan Strupczewski
item.content:encoded: The global economy is showing great resilience but there is no room for complacency, the head of the International Monetary Fund's steering committee said on Saturday, while divisions over Russia's war against Ukraine sparked a walkout of delegates. Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who heads the IMF's steering committee, asked about the walkout by nearly half of delegates during remarks by Russia's finance minister at a meeting on Saturday, said the important thing was that members ultimately agreed to the chair's statement. "We came here for a reason, and we achieved it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that's what matters," the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee told Reuters. Al-Jadaan told a press conference that the global economy was demonstrating "[USN:L1N463024 TEXT:"remarkable resilience"]" in the face of profound ongoing challenges, including wars, threats to energy and food security, high public debt levels, and risks linked to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, while warning finance officials against letting down their guard. "The message from the IMFC members is clear: There is no room for complacency," Al-Jadaan said in the final press conference of a week of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that brought more than 18,000 people to Bangkok. Fiscal authorities should work to rebuild buffers while protecting vulnerable populations and growth-enhancing investments, Al-Jadaan told reporters, underscoring the need for continued central bank independence and policies that supported private sector-led growth and investment. He said IMFC members called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by spillovers from wars and high energy prices. "International cooperation remains critical to addressing excessive global imbalances and trade tensions," he said. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva called the meetings productive but said there was clearly heightened anxiety among members about increasing divergence. Many lower income countries that were not part of the AI-value chain feared they were falling behind, she said. "These meetings also have shown that in a world of repetitive shocks and geopolitical fragmentation, still there is desire for multilateral dialogue and cooperation," she said. The Development Committee, which groups the boards of both the World Bank and the IMF, touched on similar themes in its statement, underscoring the urgent need to end wars and conflicts to ensure sustainable growth and long-term stability. "Our priority remains to promote macroeconomic and financial stability while enabling broad-based, private sector-led growth, and strengthening resilience through credible policies and international cooperation," the committee's chair, Swedish Finance Minister Elisabeth Svantesson, said. WALKOUT AMID TENSIONS Those comments came shortly after many IMFC delegates left the room when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov addressed the group in Russian. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel told a bank event on the sidelines of the meetings that nearly 50% of delegates took part in the walkout, sending a clear message to Russia. "This is a very strong signal about solidarity and values. It would be the best for the world economy if this unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine would end," Nagel said. "I was really proud so many left this plenary." Ukraine's central bank chief, Andriy Pyshnyi, told Reuters he was surprised by the large number of finance officials who left the room, calling it a [USN:L1N46303F TEXT:""deep and emotional moment.""] The Bank of England confirmed that Governor Andrew Bailey was among the delegates who joined the walkout, which comes ahead of Britain hosting the G20 next year. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who may be in the frame to take over as [USN:L6N4610XU TEXT:"chair of the World Economic Forum"], stayed in the room, two people in the meeting said. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has roiled the IMFC, preventing it from reaching consensus statements in the years since. There were deep divisions again this week as [USN:L1N46209U TEXT:"tensions flared between the US and Ukraine"]. People in the meeting said those who left while Siluanov spoke included delegates from Britain, Germany, France, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, among others. "The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe," one European diplomat said. "We cannot normalize relations with Russia." Germany on Thursday warned against efforts to [USN:L1N4610HQ TEXT:"bring Russia back"] on to the international stage after Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers, just over a month after the US hosted his first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine, at a meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. US Treasury Under Secretary Erin Browne told Reuters the same day that Washington, the current leader of the G20, supported Russia's presence. "We think it's really important if you're going to solve a crisis, you need to have open dialogue and open conversation," she told Reuters. "And you can't have ... dialogue, and you can't have resolution to conflict if no one's talking to one another." Ukraine's finance minister participated virtually in the meetings, in order to focus on budget priorities at home. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, speaking at a European Union summit on Friday, blasted US President Donald Trump's recent [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel deal"] with Russia. EU leaders have rallied around Zelenskiy after Trump again criticised Ukraine and called its strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace." Trump on Friday [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"waived"] a new congressional requirement to impose harsh sanctions on Russia.

item.title: Police and protesters clash in some of France's worst unrest in years
item.description: Authorities reported violent incidents in several cities, including vandalism in Marseille and attacks targeting police, media and public buildings.
item.dc:creator: Janis Laizans, Stamos Prousalis, Yann Tessier
item.content:encoded: Violent clashes erupted between police and protesters across France on Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of people protested against rising costs and declining public services in some of the country's most destructive unrest in years. The Interior Ministry said at least 272 people had been arrested after violent incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Toulouse in the southwest, Angers in the west and Lyon in east-central France. Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the [USN:L1N45U08J TEXT:"unrest"] on the "far-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year. "To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X. The CGT union told Agence France-Presse news agency that 800,000 people across France had taken part in Saturday's protests. The Interior Ministry did not give an estimate, and the CGT did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. "We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris. TEAR GAS, FIRE AND LOOTING In some parts of Paris, police occasionally fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas. By late afternoon, protesters reached prominent landmarks in central Paris, including the Champs-Elysees, Concorde and La Madeleine, which had been excluded from the authorised demonstration. On Saturday evening, as the protests wound down, protesters set ablaze objects including at least one car. Some tourists at a fashionable department store near the Paris opera were seen spluttering when they were caught in clouds of tear gas, and shops nearby were hastily shuttered. Windows of many shops and restaurants in the capital were smashed, and cars and trash cans were set on fire. In Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office. In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the government. In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in [USN:L6N46303L TEXT:"Brussels"], and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible. In [USN:L6N46303U TEXT:"Albania"], police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down. In [USN:L8N46304H TEXT:"Portugal"], tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe. item.title: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
item.description: The Justice Dept. said election officials could be liable as abettors of a federal crime.
item.dc:creator: Jasper Ward
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department on Friday warned Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as abettors of a federal crime if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens. The warning to the Los Angeles County Assistant Counsel Peter Bollinger came less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections and days after the department gave California [USN:L6N460192 TEXT:"48 hours"] to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action. On Thursday, the Justice Department [USN:L6N46117W TEXT:"sued California"] to block the state from counting the ballots. "Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, wrote in a letter released on Friday. McCotter called on the county and California's secretary of state to reconsider their refusal to take steps that the Trump administration argues are needed to deter voter fraud. US President Donald Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!" California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan were copied on McCotter's letter. The county's counsel office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Weber's office referred Reuters to an earlier statement in which she said the Justice Department's attempts to "unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections." An earlier letter that McCotter sent on Tuesday to Weber and Logan said the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" that were sent mail-in ballots from California. Los Angeles County Counsel Dawyn R. Harrison said on Thursday the county cannot comply with the Justice Department's requests because the Trump administration did not explain how the list was made. Friday's letter from McCotter said the Justice Department used "internal immigration records" and data matching. In July, Trump said his administration had uncovered [USN:L1N43I0TJ TEXT:"evidence"] of more than 275,000 non-citizens registered to vote, but it was not clear how many had actually voted. In some previous cases, systems intended to verify citizenship have mistakenly flagged some naturalized US citizens as noncitizens. Studies have found that noncitizens casting actual ballots is exceedingly uncommon. Since July, the Justice Department has [USN:L6N45F10R TEXT:"ramped up prosecutions"] of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. The White House has also [USN:L6N45D0T4 TEXT:"pushed"] federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

item.title: India's 'cockroach' movement founder released a day after detention
item.description: India's "cockroach" youth movement leader was released by an Indian court on Saturday, a day after he was detained for trying to lead another protest rally in New Delhi calling for the resignation of the country's election chief.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India's "cockroach" youth movement leader was released by an Indian court on Saturday, a day after he was detained for trying to lead another protest rally in New Delhi calling for the resignation of the country's election chief. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), rose to prominence this year when a weeks-long sit-in contributed to India's education minister resigning. CJP's legal affairs head Ratna Singh said Dipke was released after he agreed to certain conditions. Singh gave no details of the terms. Dipke's youth-led group, opposition parties and student organisations have held near-daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner [USN:P8N44T0DC TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar's"] resignation over a revision of [USN:L1N45V037 TEXT:"voter lists"] that they say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, who was also detained on Friday as she tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters, was released on Saturday. "Please, spare the people of India. Impeach Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured," Bora told ANI news agency after she was released. STUDENT GROUPS CALL FOR MORE PROTEST ACTION Dipke was [USN:L6N4620GJ TEXT:"detained"] on Friday as he stepped out of a house in central Delhi, with police hauling him into a police car and driving away after a brief argument. Dipke had called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban. Earlier on Friday, police had met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest. Student groups called for more protest action on Saturday. The movement, which was mobilised by the youth and joined by many opposition parties, has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges faced by Modi and the BJP in the prime minister's 12 years in power.

item.title: Zelenskiy criticizes Trump's waiver of sanctions on Russia as 'wrong'
item.description: The measures included penalties for buying Russian oil and gas.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh, Jasper Ward
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia days before they were to take effect will "unfortunately" lead to additional relief for Russia and lead to further Russian aggression, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy posted on Saturday. "The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskiy wrote on X. "It definitely helps only the Russians." An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs — including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas — that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as [USN:L6N45A18J TEXT:"the Graham Act"] that he signed into law last month. Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States. The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader. Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin and encourages more attacks by Russia. "It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people," wrote Zelenskiy, who said Russia on Friday struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites. "This certainly does not stop the war." The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. "Is Russia preparing for this? I think so," Zelenskiy wrote. Russia's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Friday called the Trump waiver "a truly historic moment," posting on X that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt. Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further [USN:L6N45A18J TEXT:"raising oil prices"] as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said. Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September. The [USN:L6N45A18J TEXT:"legislation,"] whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions. Countries such as China and [USN:L1N45G03K TEXT:"India"], which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act. Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties. But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday's executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate." US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement on Friday. Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope that there would be continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskiy, who lamented the late senator's absence. "It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," Zelenskiy posted on Saturday. The Ukrainian leader predicted that the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday's waiver and the [USN:L8N4610WB TEXT:"diesel export agreement"] announced earlier this month. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately," Zelenskiy wrote.

item.title: Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations
item.description: Bangladesh's vaccination program was a success story until it faltered because of political turmoil. Its unvaccinated children are paying the price.
item.dc:creator: Ruma Paul, Jennifer Rigby, Sam Jahan, Zia Chowdhury
item.content:encoded: Bangladesh is battling to contain the [USN:L4N44Z0Q9 TEXT:"world’s worst measles outbreak"], a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates. Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organization said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year. So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94% of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said. Bangladesh's experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95%, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped. A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents. "This is a real warning to every country," said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University. Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than [USN:L6N45R13M TEXT:"responding to an emergency"], he said. "The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died," he said. Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article. ‘THEY CAME ONLY AFTER I BURIED MY SON’ In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family's three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived. His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. "They came only after I buried my son," he said. Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition. In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine. "No health worker came to tell us," her father said. In May, Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain said the emergency drive had brought cases in hotspots "almost to zero" and the outbreak was under control. Yet in September, Bangladesh reported a daily average of 1,198 new cases of measles, which causes a high fever, cough and telltale rash. That was the highest total since May. The Bangladesh outbreak comes as [USN:L6N4560OS TEXT:"vaccine hesitancy is rising"], particularly in wealthier nations, amid skepticism championed by figures such as US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . In Bangladesh, access to inoculations and awareness are bigger hurdles, experts said. Until recently, Bangladesh had been a vaccination success story. The WHO and the United Nations children’s agency UNICEF estimated that in 2024 it achieved 96% coverage for the first vaccine dose and 93% for the second, which is given to capture the small percentage of children who don't develop immunity after one shot. But that same year, protests erupted that ended 15 years of rule by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. In the ensuing political turmoil, health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed and follow-up vaccinations that usually accompany routine programmes were disrupted. In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90%, while second-dose coverage was 86%, several percentage points below the 95% needed for herd immunity. The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025. It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100% of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers. EMERGENCY PROGRAMME MISSED MILLIONS Still, when the measles outbreak erupted, Bangladesh responded swiftly and initially seemed to be winning the battle. An emergency programme was followed by an initial slowdown in new cases after almost 20 million children received a vaccination in April and May. The government said it had covered every child in the target age group of six months to five years. But in reality the programme fell short. This emerged when another routine health intervention in June had a target list with 4 million more children than the measles campaign despite covering the same age group. "There is a gap," prime ministerial adviser Hyder told Reuters on September 14, as measles cases rose again, blaming vaccine hesitancy by parents or child illnesses for keeping kids away. Other challenges have also emerged. Documents detailing meetings in April and August between the government, the WHO and other health partners, reviewed by Reuters and not previously reported, show how efforts to act fast may have led to shortcomings. Minutes from the April 19 meeting outlined how the government opted for just one round of so-called readiness checks before launching its emergency vaccination programme due to time constraints, instead of the typical four rounds. Checks cover everything from ensuring fridges are available for keeping vaccines cool to determining how many children should be vaccinated. The single round of checks suggested most - but not all - districts were ready, according to the minutes. THE POOREST ‘PAY THE PRICE’ "When preparedness checks are not done properly, it is often the poorest and hardest-to-reach children who miss out on vaccination and pay the price," said Professor Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and chair of Bangladesh's National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination. Hyder said the April campaign was launched in four weeks. Yet Tajul Islam Abdul Bari, who led immunisation in Bangladesh until 2017, said campaigns usually demand months of planning. By the August meeting, shortcomings in the rollout were identified. Minutes noted the proportion of children with confirmed measles cases who had not been vaccinated was "virtually unchanged between pre-campaign (82%) and post-campaign (85%) ... underscoring persistent coverage gaps". The WHO did not respond to questions about the April and August meetings. But deputy WHO representative to Bangladesh, Dr Rajesh Narwal, said the WHO was determined to support the government in its goal of vaccinating every child at risk. "Routine immunisation must become more effective and resilient so that these gaps do not develop again," he said. In Sylhet, where official records show 180 children have died, 8 of 16 families Reuters interviewed in September said they had not seen health workers offering vaccinations. At least six families said health workers visited only after a child had died from measles in their community. At the end of September, the government launched a new campaign to target 3.4 million children previously missed. "We will involve people across villages so that no child is left behind," the health minister told a news conference. Yet reaching every child remains a challenge. UNICEF and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics say as many as 40% of children go unregistered, while government data showed around a third of health worker posts are unfilled. Health experts are also pushing the government to expand the programme to vaccinate children over five. That age group represents a third of measles cases, the WHO says. In addition, scientists in Bangladesh are studying why immunity is waning faster than expected in babies up to six months or so. They are usually still protected by maternal antibodies, experts say. Ensuring prompt medical care is vital, the WHO says, another challenge for Bangladesh as it also fights a [USN:L4N45N0BI TEXT:"dengue epidemic"]. In September, every ward in Sylhet's 100-bed Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital, which is treating measles, appeared overwhelmed. On the day Reuters visited, 178 patients were admitted.

item.title: White House press secretary Zacharia fired in less than a week after facing criticism
item.description: The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger weeks before the midterms.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Trevor Hunnicutt, Jasper Ward
item.content:encoded: White House press secretary [USN:FWN45V14O TEXT:"Katie Zacharia"] was fired after less than a week on the job, two US officials said on Friday, after a rocky start as President Donald Trump 's top spokesperson. Zacharia was "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to two separate White House officials. She faced days of questions about her [USN:L6N4601D0 TEXT:"legal credentials"] and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews. The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger just over two weeks before November's midterm elections , a critical period when the president is seeking to tout his administration's accomplishments and help his fellow Republicans retain control of Congress. Trump told reporters earlier on Friday that he had asked Zacharia to reconsider whether to continue in her role after facing tough press coverage during her first days on the job. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a weekend trip. He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'" Trump said he intended to revisit the conversation with Zacharia later. Zacharia started on Monday and held her debut White House briefing on Tuesday. She said she received a call about the press secretary role on October 7 and was offered the job to succeed [USN:FWN4491F6 TEXT:"Karoline Leavitt"] a week ago. She soon faced questions about her career, which she said included a tenure practicing law. Trump had also described her as an attorney. "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said in an emailed statement on Wednesday. Reuters could not find records showing the Pepperdine University law school graduate was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia. During a Fox News interview on Thursday, Zacharia said she [USN:L1N46201S TEXT:"did not pass the bar"] exam. Law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar. Zacharia and the White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about her firing. Earlier on Friday, she told reporters at the White House that she was looking forward to working with the press. Trump hired Zacharia after expressing concerns about the media coverage of his administration, feeling he needed a new spokesperson who could amplify his achievements, according to two people familiar with the conversations. In a phone interview with Fox on Friday, Trump said he was in no rush to name a new press secretary. Zacharia's quick exit meant she had what is believed to be the shortest tenure of any press secretary in the role's history. "Records are made to be broken," Anthony Scaramucci, who served as director of communications for 10 days during Trump's first administration, said on X. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

item.title: Russian strikes and winter hardship may drive more Ukrainians from homes, UN agency warns
item.description: Millions of Ukrainians face another winter of hardship as attacks on critical infrastructure, damaged housing and rising living costs threaten to force more people from their homes, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Olivia Le Poidevin
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 16 story has been corrected to say that the speaker was IOM's Arthur Erken, not Dejan Keserovic, in paragraphs 4 and 8.) Millions of Ukrainians face another winter of hardship as attacks on critical infrastructure, damaged housing and rising living costs threaten to force more people from their homes, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday. With temperatures set to fall in the coming months, many families are struggling to secure reliable heating, electricity and water after years of war, the International Organization for Migration said. This week, Russian missiles and drones have [USN:L1N46209U TEXT:"rained down on Ukrainian cities"], amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv. "Winter is fast approaching in Ukraine, and for many Ukrainians, the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began," Arthur Erken, the IOM's regional director for Europe and Central Asia, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Kyiv. Nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced across Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, while an estimated 3.8 million have returned after displacement, often to damaged or partially destroyed homes, according to the latest IOM figures. Ukrainians who returned to their homes within the last three months are the most likely to say they intend to leave again, reflecting growing concerns about deteriorating living conditions, the IOM said. European countries such as Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic currently host around 6 million Ukrainian refugees. Erken said he expected host countries to be preparing for more Ukrainians to leave if the situation got worse. Repeated Russian strikes on energy and other critical infrastructure have put increasing pressure on Ukraine's electricity, heating and water systems, while drone and missile attacks continue to kill and injure civilians across the country, the IOM said. Reliable access to water is emerging as a major concern because water systems depend heavily on electricity, the IOM said. The UN agency has installed 31 solar power stations to support water systems across Ukraine, but warned that needs remain immense. The IOM also warned that funding shortages could hamper aid efforts, with less than 7% of its 2026 Ukraine response plan funded so far, and said urgent resources were needed to improve insulation as households face freezing conditions.

item.title: Naftogaz chief says Ukraine's gas reserves hit six-year high ahead of winter
item.description: Ukrainian state oil and gas firm Naftogaz's acting CEO said the company has built its largest gas reserves in six years ahead of winter, despite a jump in Russian strikes on the company's facilities.
item.dc:creator: Pavel Polityuk
item.content:encoded: Ukrainian state oil and gas firm Naftogaz's acting CEO said the company has built its largest gas reserves in six years ahead of winter, despite a jump in Russian strikes on the company's facilities. Ukraine uses vast volumes of gas to heat its cities during the winter months, and the current season could be the most difficult of the nearly five-year war with Russia, which has sharply intensified its attacks on Ukraine's energy sector. The attacks also put at risk the colossal Soviet-era power stations which Ukrainian cities rely on for winter heat. Naftogaz CEO Sergii Fedorenko told Reuters Russia had attacked Naftogaz assets more than 400 times so far this year, twice as many times as in 2025. "This year, most of our facilities have come under attack," Fedorenko said, adding that oil and gas production, processing and transportation facilities, as well as thermal power plants in frontline regions, have been hit. "We are strengthening defences and digging in," he said. RESERVES AT 16 BILLION CUBIC METRES, NAFTOGAZ SAYS Fedorenko said Naftogaz had managed to bring the volume of reserves in underground storage facilities to 16 billion cubic metres, the highest since 2020. Ukraine began the previous heating season with reserves of less than 14 bcm. The government has said the country needed at least 13.2 bcm of gas in reserve to get through the winter. The rise in reserves comes as consumption has fallen this year, largely because Russian strikes on industrial infrastructure have already forced the shutdown of some factories. Fedorenko estimates that gas consumption in 2026 will fall to about 20 bcm from 21 bcm in 2025. He said it is difficult to make predictions during a war, when everything can change at any moment. "By the start of the heating season, we keep restoring and restoring our destroyed production," he said. "We look forward with caution. Every morning I wake up and check my phone to see if any of our facilities were hit overnight." Ukrainian legislation prohibits state-owned companies from disclosing data on the results of their operations in the energy sector. COLD WEATHER, RUSSIAN STRIKES DROVE IMPORTS TO A RECORD Ukraine is a net gas importer. Since 2015 it has stopped buying Russian gas directly, instead importing from European suppliers, primarily via Poland, Slovakia, and Hungary. Heavy frosts and Russian strikes on underground storage facilities forced Naftogaz to import a record 7.8 bcm of gas in 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, Fedorenko said. This season, it started buying gas early and has so far contracted more than 1 bcm of imports, 25% of which is LNG. "We contracted supplies specifically for the heating season, meaning we have contracts for delivery during a defined period — December through March," Fedorenko said. Ukraine operates Europe's largest underground gas storage facilities, with capacity of about 30 bcm, and Fedorenko said Kyiv has proposed that the EU store part of its gas reserves there, allocating one-third of the capacity for that purpose. Located more than 1 km underground, the gas is protected from attacks and can, if needed, be delivered very quickly to consumers, particularly in Eastern European countries, Fedorenko said. He said the Ukrainian gas storage tariff is currently the lowest in the EU.

item.title: AI jitters, Trump's fading oil clout and China shock 2.0: The financial week in five charts
item.description: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days.
item.dc:creator: Anna Szymanski
item.content:encoded: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest (ROI) distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days. AI DOMINANCE JAMIE MCGEEVER, ROI Markets Columnist: What goes up must ... keep going up? That has largely been the case for AI-related stocks since OpenAI launched ChatGPT nearly four years ago. JPMorgan Private Bank's Michael Cembalest reckons AI-related stocks have accounted for 75% of S&P 500 returns, 80% of earnings growth and 90% of capital-spending growth since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. But the stock-market boom is [USN:L6N45Y0TW TEXT:"not necessarily translating"] into an equally powerful economic one for the US. And concerns are mounting over the scale of AI investment, how it is funded and whether it will ultimately deliver adequate returns. Perhaps what goes up must come down. Eventually. 2. DEBT STRAIN ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: The [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US Consumer Price Index"] rose 0.6% last month, faster than the 0.4% increase in August, bringing the 12-month rate to 3.7%, largely due to a 9.1% rise in gasoline prices. More worrying for markets, however, was the core inflation reading, which strips out food and energy. It jumped 0.3% in September, slightly above economists' consensus forecast, driven by notable increases in housing costs and airline fares. This heightened concerns that US interest rates will stay higher for longer as the Federal Reserve seeks to return inflation to its 2% target. That, in turn, caused investors to flee — or hedge — some of the [USN:L4N46111C TEXT:"more heavily indebted AI companies"], which may struggle to generate enough cash to service higher debt costs. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , the AI-focused cloud-computing firm, was among the biggest losers on Thursday. Its 5-year credit default swap surged past 1,100 basis points at one point, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence, while the yield on the company's 2031 bond rose to as high as 16% before retreating. 3. DIMINISHING POWER RON BOUSSO, ROI Energy Columnist: US President Donald Trump's trademark ability to [USN:L6N45Y0SD TEXT:"talk down oil markets"] with a few words is fading as the Iran war drags on, leaving global energy prices far more exposed to escalation. The market's muted reaction to Trump's diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin is the latest example. This reflects a deeper problem. The loss of around 2 million barrels per day of refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East, and the sharp drawdown in global oil inventories since the start of the Iran war, have left energy markets in a precarious position that cannot be fixed through rhetoric or relatively small supply additions. 4. EXPORT BLITZ MIKE DOLAN, ROI Finance & Markets Columnist: China's trade surplus widened more than expected in September as [USN:AZN4TOTAU TEXT:"exports surged"], stoking anxiety in Europe and elsewhere about a "China shock 2.0" as more of the country's goods flow into overseas markets. Strong demand for semiconductors and green-tech products has kept China's factories humming. Exports jumped 36% from a year earlier — the fastest pace since February — up from 25% in August and well above forecasts for 26% growth. Import growth also beat expectations, but the trade surplus still reached $938 billion in the first nine months. It is now on track to top $1 trillion a month earlier than last year, adding to [USN:L6N45Y0XV TEXT:"pressure on Europe"] to push for a stronger yuan and fairer competition. 5. ASIAN EDGE GAVIN MAGUIRE, ROI Global Energy Transition Columnist: Oil supplies are recovering faster than fuel output in the Middle East, where several regional refineries remain offline after sustaining damage during the conflict with Iran. That bodes well for refiners in Asia, home to more refining capacity than any other region. The massive coastal complexes in India, China, South Korea and Singapore were built to receive crude oil in bulk and convert it into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel for global markets. If Middle Eastern crude exports continue to rise, [USN:L1N45S14J TEXT:"Asian refiners appear well positioned"] to capture much of the value created by turning those barrels into the fuels that power the global economy. item.title: World's rarest porpoise battles extinction as Mexico shrinks protected area
item.description: Mexico drastically reduced the protected area for the vaquita marina.
item.dc:creator: Ana Martinez, Sarah Morland
item.content:encoded: Mexico's president said on Thursday a drastic reduction in the protected area for the near-extinct vaquita marina, the world's smallest porpoise, will help fishing communities. Critics say this week's reduction in the area where fishermen cannot use gillnets, long walls of nylon mesh, by 86% to 1,562 square kilometers (603 square miles), about the size of Greater London, threatens the survival of the species. The prior agreement had protected an area similar to the size of the US state of Connecticut. President Claudia Sheinbaum said the new scope aimed to protect biodiversity in the Gulf of California while also allowing fishermen to make a better living. Authorities said the measure took into account proposals by the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita, a government advisory body. Lorenzo Rojas-Bracho, a Mexican marine biologist and leading vaquita expert who took part in the committee, said he hoped a smaller area could concentrate efforts to save the mammal. "It is difficult to enforce a ban over a very large area, which includes vast areas with no recent records of vaquitas," Rojas-Bracho told Reuters. "If you lose a ring you don't search your entire house, you focus on where you lost it." Scientists estimated last year there were just 7 to 10 vaquitas left, including at least one calf. The population has collapsed from around 600 in 1997, largely due to illegal fishing targeting totoaba, whose swim bladders are highly prized in Chinese medicine and can fetch up to $10,000 in Asia. Rojas-Bracho said that if no more vaquitas are killed, the remaining handful of porpoises would have a good chance of repopulating the species. However, he said the area needs more effective tracking of fishing boats, better monitoring and that fishermen should use alternative methods that do not put the vaquita at risk. Gerardo Ceballos, a biologist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, said allowing the vaquita to become extinct would amount to a moral failure. "What's happening to the vaquita is a death foretold," he said. "We've reduced the vaquita's protected area without actually having the technical or logistical capacity to enforce regulations there; we're giving in to pressure from interested groups so a larger area can be exploited." Ceballos said a very minimal government investment would ensure the vaquita's protection. As things currently stood, however, he believed the porpoise was on the path to extinction. "If the vaquita goes extinct it won't solve insecurity or poverty or any of the local problems. And Mexico would lose an icon," he said. "If actions are taken, there is a possibility, a hope. And we must keep working with hope."

item.title: Could hackers get inside my fridge?
item.description: An expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Lhomedet, Leo Marchandon
item.content:encoded: Hackers who [USN:L8N45Y11U TEXT:"sabotaged"] refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets exploited the growing connectivity of equipment that was once largely mechanical. From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals. CAN HACKERS REALLY GET INTO MY FRIDGE? In theory, yes. If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked. In 2015, researchers demonstrated at a Las Vegas hacking conference how a Samsung smart refrigerator could be compromised, allowing them to intercept some of the internet traffic passing through the device. In many cases, attackers are more interested in stealing data, disrupting services or using connected devices as a way into a larger network. WHAT HOUSEHOLD DEVICES COULD BE HACKED? The most common targets are devices connected to the internet and controlled remotely. These include security cameras, video doorbells, alarm systems, smart locks, thermostats and central heating systems. Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens and washing machines can also be vulnerable if they are connected to the wider internet. Even some toothbrushes are now internet-connected. Routers, not appliances, account for more than three-quarters of all attacks on connected devices, according to security-industry data. The number of such devices has grown rapidly as manufacturers have added internet connectivity to products that were once entirely mechanical. WHAT COULD A HACKER ACTUALLY DO? Once inside a device, a hacker can generally do one of two things: gather information or take control of the device. A camera can show the inside of a home, a device with a microphone can pick up sound, and a compromised router can expose everything that travels through the network. Hackers who take control of a device can switch it on or off, change settings or lock users out of their accounts. A compromised thermostat could affect heating, while a hacked freezer or refrigerator could disrupt temperature controls. In more serious cases, attackers may use poorly secured devices to gain access to other systems on the same network or to steal personal information linked to online accounts. COULD HACKERS TAKE OVER MY CAR, ELECTRICITY OR WATER SUPPLY? Cybersecurity researchers have repeatedly demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles. In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes. Nearly a decade later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only a licence plate number. The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited in real-world attacks. Modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems. Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that are not present in consumer devices. That does not mean they are immune from cyber attacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi‑Fi network. HOW CAN PEOPLE PROTECT THEIR DEVICES? Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available and regularly installing software updates. Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so. The simplest rule is often the most effective: the fewer connected devices you have, the fewer potential entry points exist for attackers.
